stages.title: Advanced vocabulary and terminology
stages.hook: Why do Turkish speakers say 'uçak' for airplane, while older texts say 'tayyare'?
explain: After 1932 the Turkish Language Association (Türk Dil Kurumu, TDK) promoted native Turkish words in place of many Arabic and Persian loans: 'tayyare' became 'uçak', 'müsabaka' became 'yarışma', 'hâdise' became 'olay'. Many Arabic and Persian words remain in daily use, e.g. kitap, saat, dünya, sebep.

Advanced vocabulary often forms words from roots with derivational suffixes: -lik (abstract noun: güzellik, beauty), -ci (occupation: gazeteci, journalist), -siz (without: sessiz, silent), -li (with: akıllı, clever). Compounds: 'bilgisayar' (computer; bilgi + say-), 'yazılım' (software), 'donanım' (hardware). Register matters: 'dünya' is neutral, while 'cihan' is literary.
stages.mnemonic: Root plus suffix gives a family: göz, gözlük, gözcü.
sentences: The software was developed in Turkey.

gq.q: What does the suffix -ci often form?

panel.q: Why did TDK replace 'tayyare' with 'uçak'?
o: To borrow more words from English during the 1932 reform
To favour native Turkish roots in the 1932 language reform
Because tayyare was a spelling mistake in older books
To simplify the spelling of Arabic words in the 1932 reform
panel.why: The language reform replaced many loanwords.

panel.q: Which pair shows a derivation with -lik?
panel.why: -lik forms abstract nouns.

panel.q: Why does register matter for 'cihan' vs 'dünya'?
o: They are identical in meaning and in register
Cihan is slang and dünya is formal only
Dünya is old and cihan is the modern word
Cihan is literary and dünya is neutral
panel.why: Word choice signals style.

teach.model: Use roots and suffixes to build words: -lik, -ci, -siz, -li. Learn the 1932 language reform and register difference.

stages.title: Academic language
stages.hook: How do academic writers avoid 'I' in Turkish research papers?
explain: Academic Turkish prefers the passive voice and impersonal forms: 'Bu çalışmada ... incelenmiştir' (In this study ... was examined). The passive is formed with -ıl/-il/-ul/-ül after a consonant, -n after a vowel and -ın/-in after l: yapıldı (was done), yazıldı (was written), görüldü (was seen), incelendi (was examined). Nominalisation with -ma/-me gives 'çalışma' (study), 'araştırma' (research).

Common academic terms: 'amaç' (aim), 'yöntem' (method), 'bulgular' (findings), 'sonuç' (conclusion), 'kaynakça' (bibliography), 'özet' (abstract), 'makale' (article), 'bildiri' (conference paper). Hedging: 'görülmektedir' (it is seen), 'olabilir' (may be), 'öne sürülebilir' (it may be argued). Citations use author, year, and page.
stages.mnemonic: Passive and impersonal: the study speaks, not 'I'.
sentences: The method was explained in the study.
The findings are shown in the table.
The aim of this study is clear.

gq.q: How is the passive formed in 'yapıldı'?

panel.q: Why use the passive in an abstract?
o: To make the abstract shorter than the paper
Because Turkish has no first person at all
To keep the tone impersonal and objective
To avoid verbs and use only nouns
panel.why: Impersonal passive suits academic register.

panel.q: Which phrase is a hedge?
panel.why: It suggests tentative claim.

panel.q: What does '-ma/-me' do in 'araştırma'?
o: Turns a verb into a noun
Turns a noun into a verb form
Makes a plural noun from a singular
Makes the verb negative or past
panel.why: Nominalisation.

teach.model: Use passive and impersonal forms: incelenmiştir. Key terms: amaç, yöntem, bulgular, sonuç, kaynakça. Hedge claims with -ebilir.

trip.prompt: Study the structure of an abstract.

stages.title: Professional communication
stages.hook: How do you write a Turkish email that asks for a job interview?
explain: Professional Turkish uses polite formulas. Email opening: 'Sayın Yetkili,' closing: 'Saygılarımla'. Phrases: 'Ekte özgeçmişimi gönderiyorum' (I attach my CV), 'Başvurumu değerlendirmenizi rica ederim' (I request that you consider my application), 'Bilgilerinize sunarım' (I submit this for your information), 'Gereğini rica ederim' (I request that necessary action be taken).

Workplace vocabulary: iş görüşmesi (job interview), özgeçmiş (CV), sözleşme (contract), maaş (salary), toplantı (meeting), müdür (manager), şirket (company). In meetings use 'söz almak' (to take the floor), 'gündem' (agenda) and 'karar' (decision). Keep sentences clear and avoid slang.
stages.mnemonic: Sayın, ekte, rica ederim, saygılarımla: the formal frame.

gq.q: What does 'ekte' mean in an email?

panel.q: Which opening suits an unknown recipient?
panel.why: Formal address.

panel.q: Why use 'rica ederim' in a request?
o: It is slang used between close friends
It means only 'thanks' in every case
It turns the sentence into a question
panel.why: Rica ederim literally means 'I request' and turns a demand into a formal, polite request, which suits messages to people you do not know. (Said in reply to thanks, it also means 'you are welcome'.)

panel.q: Why mention 'gündem' before a meeting?
o: It is the time of the meeting
It is the place of the meeting
It is a gift for the chair
panel.why: Agenda.

teach.model: In formal emails use Sayın Yetkili, ekte, rica ederim and Saygılarımla. Workplace words: özgeçmiş, sözleşme, gündem.

points.ask: How do I frame an email?
How do I attach a file?
How do I make a request?

stages.title: Literary analysis
stages.hook: What can a novel's narrator reveal about the story in Turkish literature?
explain: Literary analysis looks at narrator (anlatıcı), theme (tema), character (karakter), setting (mekân), time (zaman) and style (üslup). Yaşar Kemal's İnce Memed (1955) follows a village boy who becomes an outlaw in the Taurus region. Orhan Pamuk's Benim Adım Kırmızı (1998) is told by many voices, including a corpse and a colour. Sabahattin Ali's Kürk Mantolu Madonna is a love story told through a diary.

Poetry: Nazım Hikmet used free verse; Orhan Veli and the Garip movement (1941) used everyday speech. Ask: Who speaks? What changes? What images repeat? 'Birinci kişi anlatıcı' (first-person narrator) limits knowledge to one view; 'üçüncü kişi' (third-person narrator) can know more.
stages.mnemonic: Who speaks? What image repeats? What changes?
sentences: The poem has a strong theme.
The setting is a small village.

gq.why: İnce Memed is by Yaşar Kemal.

gq.q: Which movement used everyday speech in poetry in 1941?

panel.q: Why does a first-person narrator limit the reader?
o: The reader only knows what the narrator knows
The narrator knows everything about all characters
There is no narrator in a first-person story
Poetry is the only genre with a narrator
panel.why: Point of view limits information.

panel.q: Which question helps analyse a poem?
panel.why: Repeated images reveal meaning.

panel.q: What does Benim Adım Kırmızı do formally?
panel.why: It has multiple voices.

teach.model: Identify narrator, theme, character, setting and style. Ask who speaks and what image repeats.

points.ask: What do I look for in a poem?

stages.title: Advanced listening comprehension
stages.hook: How can you catch the main idea of a fast news report in Turkish?
explain: News reports use compact language and many connectors: 'ancak', 'bu nedenle' (for this reason), 'ayrıca', 'buna karşın' (in contrast). Listen first for the subject and the final verb, then numbers and names. Reported speech uses 'dedi' or 'açıkladı' (said, announced) and the evidential -miş for uncertain information: 'Yarın yağmur yağacakmış' (They say it will rain tomorrow).

Predict content: if the topic is the economy, expect 'enflasyon', 'faiz', 'büyüme'. Note signal words for contrast and cause. Because Turkish is verb-final, the key action arrives last: wait for it. Repeated listening helps with unfamiliar accents.
stages.mnemonic: Wait for the verb, listen for the connector.
sentences: They say it will rain tomorrow.

o: Certainty: the speaker saw it happen
A past event that the speaker saw
A question about what will happen

gq.why: Bu nedenle introduces a cause or consequence, as in for this reason.

panel.q: Why wait for the end of the sentence?
panel.why: Turkish puts the verb last, so the main action only arrives at the end of the clause.

panel.q: What strategy helps with numbers?
o: Ignore them and wait for the verb
Translate all of them into English
Write down every word you hear
panel.why: Figures and units usually carry the key facts of a news item, so catch them first.

panel.q: Why predict the topic before listening?
o: It replaces the need to listen
It is a way of cheating
panel.why: Expecting words such as enflasyon or faiz lets you recognise them quickly in fast speech.

teach.model: Listen for connectors, subject and the final verb. -miş marks reported information. Predict vocabulary from the topic.

stages.title: Oral fluency and presentations
stages.hook: How do you keep talking when you forget a word?
explain: Fluent speakers use fillers and repair strategies: 'yani' (I mean), 'şey' (thing, um), 'demek istediğim' (what I mean is), 'başka bir deyişle' (in other words). If you forget a word, describe it: 'o şey, yazı yazdığımız...' Self-correction: 'yani, daha doğrusu...' (rather, more precisely).

In an oral presentation: signpost with 'Öncelikle ...', 'Bunun yanı sıra ...' (in addition), 'Özetle ...' (in short). Control pace and use intonation: In yes/no questions the pitch peaks on the syllable just before the particle mi, and statements generally fall at the end. Use gestures and eye contact.
stages.mnemonic: If you lose a word, describe it.
sentences: In other words, it is simple.

gq.why: Daha doğrusu corrects or sharpens what you just said.

panel.q: Why describe a forgotten word?
o: It is wrong and shows weak Turkish
It wastes time during the whole talk
It is rude to the audience
panel.why: Describing the missing word (circumlocution) keeps you speaking instead of stopping.

panel.q: What do signposts do in a talk?
panel.why: Words like öncelikle and özetle tell listeners where you are in the talk.

panel.q: Why control your pace in a presentation?
o: The audience can follow and understand
Faster speech is always better for experts
It hides mistakes in grammar and spelling
It removes the need for a clear structure
panel.why: A steady pace helps listeners process what they hear.

teach.model: Use fillers sparingly, repair with daha doğrusu, signpost with öncelikle and özetle. Describe words you forget.

points.ask: What if I forget a word?

stages.title: Translation and interpretation
stages.hook: What is the difference between an interpreter and a translator in Turkish?
explain: A translator (çevirmen) works with written text; an interpreter (tercüman) works with spoken language. Consecutive interpreting (ardıl çeviri) happens in pauses; simultaneous interpreting (eşzamanlı çeviri) happens at the same time, often in a booth.

Problems: Turkish is SOV, so in simultaneous interpreting you often wait for the verb. Strategies: chunk, summarise, and keep the register. Terminology must be consistent: 'veri' (data), 'yapay zekâ' (artificial intelligence). Honorifics and politeness (siz, Bey, Hanım) must be reflected. Cultural items like 'Eline sağlık' need functional equivalents.
stages.mnemonic: Çevirmen for the page, tercüman for the voice.
sentences: The interpreter works in the booth.

gq.why: A tercüman interprets speech, while a çevirmen works on written text.

o: After the speaker has finished a section
In writing, long after the event
Before the speaker begins to talk
At the same time as the speaker
gq.why: Eşzamanlı çeviri means the interpreter speaks while the speaker is still talking.

panel.q: Why is verb-final order hard for interpreters?
o: The verbs are too short to hear
panel.why: The verb comes last, so the interpreter may have to wait for it before giving the full meaning.

panel.q: How do you handle honorifics?
o: Reflect politeness in the target language
Ignore them because Turkish is informal
Remove them from the translation altogether
panel.why: Siz, titles and polite forms carry social meaning, so the target text must show the same level of respect.

panel.q: Why keep terminology consistent?
panel.why: If one concept has two names, readers may think there are two concepts.

teach.model: Translators handle text; interpreters handle speech. Consecutive and simultaneous modes differ. Watch verb-final order, register and terminology.

points.ask: Why is Turkish hard to interpret?

stages.title: Idiomatic and figurative language
stages.hook: What does 'ağzı kulaklarında' tell us about someone?
explain: Figurative language is rich in Turkish. 'Ağzı kulaklarında' (his mouth is at his ears) means grinning from ear to ear. 'Gözü yükseklerde' means ambitious. 'Burnu havada' means arrogant. 'Kulak asmak' means to pay attention, usually in the negative: 'kulak asmadı' (he ignored it).

Proverbs: 'Damlaya damlaya göl olur' (drop by drop a lake forms: little things add up), 'Ayağını yorganına göre uzat' (stretch your legs according to your quilt: live within your means), 'Ne ekersen onu biçersin' (you reap what you sow). Never translate idioms literally; map them to a similar idea in the target language.
stages.mnemonic: Body parts hide meanings: ağız, göz, burun, kulak.
items: Drop by drop a lake forms
sentences: He was grinning from ear to ear.
Little by little, it becomes a lake.

gq.why: The image is a nose held high in the air, which stands for arrogance.

gq.q: Which proverb says little things add up?
gq.why: The saying means that small amounts add up to something big.

panel.q: Why not translate idioms word for word?
panel.why: Idioms mean something different from their words, so a literal version confuses or amuses the reader.

panel.q: Which proverb advises living modestly?
o: Damlaya damlaya göl olur (little by little)
Ne ekersen onu biçersin (you reap what you sow)
panel.why: The picture of stretching legs only as far as the quilt reaches means living within your means.

panel.q: What does 'kulak asmadı' mean?
panel.why: Kulak asmak is usually used in the negative, so kulak asmadı means he ignored it.

teach.model: Many idioms use body parts. Proverbs give advice. Translate by meaning, not words.

stages.title: Extended independent writing
stages.hook: How can you plan a 500-word essay in Turkish?
explain: Plan the thesis (tez), arguments (argümanlar), counterargument (karşı görüş) and conclusion (sonuç). A typical outline: giriş (hook, thesis), gelişme (2–3 paragraphs, each with a claim and evidence), karşı görüş (the other side) and sonuç. Use paragraphs with topic sentences and linking: 'Öte yandan' (on the other hand), 'Bununla birlikte' (nevertheless), 'Dolayısıyla' (consequently).

Check cohesion: pronouns refer clearly; tense is consistent; subordination uses participles (-dığı için, -mesi nedeniyle). Edit: remove repetition, vary sentence length, check apostrophes on proper names, vowel harmony, and punctuation. A clear conclusion restates the thesis without repeating sentences.
sentences: On the other hand, costs rise.
Consequently, we need a new plan.

gq.q: Which word means 'on the other hand'?
gq.why: Öte yandan presents a different side of the argument.
A counterargument is the view that opposes the thesis.

panel.q: Why include a counterargument?
o: It only makes the essay longer
It is required by every grader
It confuses the reader about the thesis
panel.why: Answering the other side makes the essay fairer and more convincing.

panel.q: Which sentence supports cohesion?
o: A pronoun with a clear referent
Many fillers such as yani and şey
panel.why: Pronouns work only when it is clear who or what they refer to.

panel.q: Why edit last?
o: To add new content and sources
To fix style and harmony errors
panel.why: Editing is for fixing style, repetition, harmony and punctuation once the content is settled.

teach.model: Plan thesis, arguments, counterargument and conclusion. Link with öte yandan, bununla birlikte, dolayısıyla. Edit for harmony and punctuation.
